summary: Bulgaria lies in the eastern Balkan Peninsula on the western shore of the Black Sea, is one of the birthplaces of the Cyrillic alphabet, and is known for rose oil and yogurt.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In 864 Boris I of the First Bulgarian Empire accepted baptism from Byzantium, and in 886 he received the disciples of Cyril and Methodius and held services in Slavonic, making Eastern Orthodoxy the state religion. During Ottoman rule from 1396 to 1878 the Church was an important force in preserving the Bulgarian language and national identity, and in 1870 the Bulgarian Church became independent of the Greek-dominated Patriarchate of Constantinople. Religion was suppressed in the communist period (1944-1989), so although the majority identify with Orthodoxy, the share who actually take part in religious activities is not high.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived with the Ottoman conquest at the end of the 14th century; its adherents are mainly ethnic Turks, the Islamized Bulgarians known as Pomaks, and some Roma, concentrated in the northeast and in the Rhodope Mountains of the south. In 1984-1989 the communist regime carried out the 'Revival Process', forcing Muslims to adopt Slavic names, and in 1989 more than 300,000 ethnic Turks were forced to move to Turkey, which lowered the Muslim share.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population stems mainly from the atheist education and religious suppression carried out by the communist regime of 1944-1989, and many who grew up in this period have no religious belief. Although there has been a religious revival since 1989, young city dwellers have been affected by secularization, and some still identify as having no religion or did not answer the question about religion.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in the 19th century by American Congregationalist and Methodist missionaries, who took part in the translation of the Bible into Bulgarian in the 1860s and in 1860 founded the American College in Plovdiv (now the American College of Sofia), which influenced Bulgarian education. In the communist period Protestant pastors were put on show trial in 1949, and after independence Pentecostalism has also grown, but overall it still accounts for only about 1 percent.

religion.background: The Bulgarian region in ancient times was the territory of the Thracians, and Christianity had already arrived in the 4th century in the Roman Empire. In 864 Boris I accepted Christianity, and at the end of the 9th century the Cyrillic alphabet developed in Bulgaria, making Bulgaria one of the centers of Slavic Orthodox culture. Nearly five hundred years of Ottoman rule from 1396 brought Islam, and the inhabitants of some areas converted. After independence in 1878 Eastern Orthodoxy became the state church, religion was suppressed in the communist period, and the 1991 constitution guarantees religious freedom and recognizes Eastern Orthodoxy as the 'traditional religion'.

ranking.name: Bulgarian
ranking.description: Bulgarian belongs to the South Slavic group; after the Slavs and the Turkic Bulgars founded a state here in the 7th century, Slavic gradually became the national language. At the end of the 9th century the disciples of Cyril and Methodius developed the Cyrillic alphabet in Bulgaria, making Old Bulgarian (Old Church Slavonic) the written language of the whole Orthodox Slavic world. Today about 85 percent of the population speak it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish speakers are the ethnic Turkish minority of Bulgaria, whose ancestors moved in after the Ottoman conquest of 1396 or converted locally. After independence in 1878 ethnic Turks repeatedly moved to Turkey, and the forced assimilation policy of the communist regime in 1989 drove out some 300,000 people. Today they are concentrated in Shumen and Razgrad in the northeast and in Kardzhali in the south.

ranking.name: Romani
ranking.description: Romani is the language of the Roma (Gypsies), whose ancestors migrated west from northern India about 1,000 years ago and had appeared in the Balkans before the 14th century. Bulgaria is one of the European countries with the highest share of Roma, but they have long been on the margins of society, and many Roma children cannot study in their mother tongue at school.

language.history: The Slavs moved into the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries, and in 681 the Bulgars founded the First Bulgarian Empire, later merging with the Slavs and adopting the Slavic language. At the end of the 9th century the Cyrillic alphabet developed in the literary schools of Preslav and Ohrid, and Old Bulgarian became the church language of the Slavic world of Eastern Europe; 24 May is still the 'Day of Slavonic Script and Bulgarian Culture'. During Ottoman rule Bulgarian absorbed a great deal of Turkish vocabulary, and the national revival movement of the 19th century promoted the establishment of a standard language. In 2007 Bulgaria joined the European Union, and the Cyrillic alphabet thus also became one of the official scripts of the EU.

ranking.name: Banitsa
ranking.description: A savory pie baked with layers of thin filo pastry wrapped around eggs, yogurt and white cheese (sirene); the crust is crisp and the inside moist, and it is often served with a yogurt drink.
ranking.history: Banitsa belongs to the Balkan family of filo pastries and is related to the 'börek' technique that came during the Ottoman period, but Bulgarians regard banitsa with a white cheese filling as their most representative national food. On New Year's Eve and at Christmas, Bulgarian families hide slips of paper with wishes or coins in the banitsa, and whoever gets one symbolizes good luck in the coming year. It is also Bulgaria's most common breakfast and street snack.

ranking.name: Shopska Salad
ranking.description: A refreshing salad of diced tomato, cucumber, onion and roasted sweet pepper, topped with plenty of grated white cheese and dressed with vegetable oil and vinegar.
ranking.history: Shopska salad is not an ancient traditional dish but a dish designed in the 1950s and 60s, in the communist period, by the state tourism company 'Balkantourist' to promote tourism. Its red, green and white colors happen to match the Bulgarian flag, and its name is taken from the inhabitants of the Shop region around Sofia. It quickly became Bulgaria's most famous dish, and in 2014 it was chosen as Bulgaria's representative dish in a European Union promotional campaign.

ranking.name: Tarator
ranking.description: A cold soup of yogurt diluted with water, with chopped cucumber, garlic, dill and walnuts, drunk chilled; it is light and slightly sour.
ranking.history: Tarator is a food for beating the heat in Bulgaria's hot summers, based on the yogurt of which Bulgarians are proud. In 1905 the Bulgarian medical student Stamen Grigorov discovered the lactic acid bacteria in yogurt (later named Lactobacillus bulgaricus), and then the Russian scientist Metchnikoff linked the longevity of Bulgarian peasants with eating yogurt, making Bulgarian yogurt famous around the world. Tarator has therefore also become representative of Bulgarian food culture.

ranking.name: Kebapche
ranking.description: Ground pork and beef are mixed with cumin, salt and black pepper, shaped into long sausages and charcoal-grilled, charred outside and juicy inside, often served with fries and salad.
ranking.history: The name kebapche is related to the Ottoman grilling tradition, but the modern version is said to have been invented in the 1920s when a cook at a Sofia restaurant, while grilling, improvised by shaping ground meat into long sausages. Because Bulgaria is an Orthodox country, pork is often added, unlike the grilled meat made with lamb and beef in the neighboring Islamic countries. It is the most common dish at Bulgarian grill houses and beer halls, often ordered together with kyufte (grilled meatballs).

ranking.name: Lyutenitsa
ranking.description: A thick spread cooked from roasted red peppers, tomatoes, eggplant and garlic, bright red and slightly sweet, often spread on bread or served with meat.
ranking.history: Tomatoes and sweet peppers are native to the Americas and entered the Balkans through the Mediterranean after the 16th century, and from the 19th century Bulgaria became an important vegetable-growing region of Europe. Making lyutenitsa is a traditional autumn family activity, in which each household roasts red peppers in the yard, cooks the sauce and puts it into glass jars to keep through the winter. In the communist period state factories began to mass-produce it, but many families still insist on making it themselves every autumn.
